opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the beginning I was a bit lost, because my background wasn't in language models. I came from physics, and theoretical physics trains you to think very differently. So when the interview came up, I realized I didn't even know what a good answer would look like, let alone how to prepare for it.

What I ended up doing was going back to first principles, which is the physicist's habit. Instead of memorizing a list of tricks or the latest papers, I asked: what actually happens when you train a language model? What's the data, what's the objective, where does compute go, what tends to break? I tried to rebuild the whole pipeline in my head, from pretraining through post-training, and for each piece I asked why it's done that way and what would happen if you changed it.

Then I read a lot, but in a targeted way. I picked a small number of foundational papers and some practical write-ups from people who had actually trained large models, and I tried to understand them well enough to explain them to someone else. If I couldn't explain why a certain design choice mattered, I didn't really understand it yet.

I also talked to friends who were already working in the field. That helped a lot, because the knowledge that matters in practice, like what people actually worry about day to day, isn't always written down. Hearing how they think about problems gave me a sense of the taste and intuition the interviewers were probably looking for.

And I accepted that I wouldn't know everything. In the interview I tried to be honest about what I didn't know, and to show how I would reason through it. I think that's what they cared about more: not whether you've memorized the answer, but whether you can think clearly about a problem you haven't seen before. In a field that moves this fast, that's most of the job anyway.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes studying training fundamentals, reading papers and write-ups, and talking with practitioners, but does not say they personally implemented a small GPT model.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't really know how to prepare, and I think that's the truthful answer. My background at Princeton was mostly on the agent side, on reasoning, things like ReAct and Tree of Thoughts, and that's a very different world from large-scale pretraining or post-training infrastructure. So when I started talking to labs about model training roles, I had this moment of, okay, what does this interview even test?

What I ended up doing was fairly simple. First, I went back to basics. I reread the fundamental papers, the Transformer paper, the scaling-law papers, the RLHF and instruction-tuning work, and I tried to actually re-derive things rather than just recognize them. There's a big gap between having read something and being able to explain why a design choice was made and what would break if you changed it. I spent a lot of time on that gap.

Second, I tried to think about training from the perspective of the problems that matter, not the topics. Instead of memorizing techniques, I asked myself: if I had to make a model better at reasoning, or better at using tools, what would I actually change in the data, in the reward, in the evaluation? That framing helped, because it turned preparation into something closer to research than studying for an exam.

And third, I accepted that I couldn't fake experience I didn't have. I hadn't trained a frontier model. So I leaned into what I did know deeply, which was agents and reasoning, and tried to show how that connects to training, how you'd generate the right environments, how you'd evaluate, where the bottlenecks really are. I think the interviewers cared less about whether I knew every trick and more about whether I could think clearly about an open problem.

Looking back, the lack of a clear recipe was probably fine. In this field the questions change so fast that the real skill is being able to reason from first principles when nobody has told you what to study.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes rereading and re-deriving papers and reasoning about training problems, but does not say they personally implemented a small GPT model.

astra-6.text: I didn’t really know what to study, so I treated the interview as a chance to learn. I went in, tried to answer the questions, and paid attention to where I got stuck. That gave me a much clearer idea of what I needed to understand. Then I could go back, fill those gaps, and be better prepared the next time.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes using the interview to identify knowledge gaps and study them afterward, but does not mention personally implementing a small GPT model.

sol-6.1.text: I didn’t really have a clear preparation plan. I would start by asking what I understood well enough to explain, and where I was just recognizing terminology. Then I’d try to fill those gaps—work through the reasoning, think about how I would run an experiment, and what I’d do if the result was unexpected. Without knowing exactly what to prepare, that seemed more useful than trying to predict the questions.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes identifying knowledge gaps and reasoning through experiments, but does not say they personally implemented a small GPT model.
